Add the voltage drops along the path from A to B: two resistors and the forward-biased
diode.
**Step 1 — note the current.** The same **0·2 mA** flows through the whole series path,
since the capacitor branch carries no steady current ✓
**Step 2 — find the drop across each resistor.**
V = IR = (0·2 x 10⁻³)(5 x 10³)
= **1 V** across each ✓
and there are two of them, giving **2 V** in total.
**Step 3 — add the diode's drop.** A forward-biased diode drops a nearly constant
**0·2 V**, as stated ✓
**Step 4 — total.**
V_AB = 1 + 0·2 + 1
= **2·2 V** ✓
**Why the capacitor is irrelevant.** In the steady state a capacitor passes **no
current** ✓ Its branch can be ignored entirely for this calculation - it is in the
circuit to see whether that is recognised.
**Why the diode's drop is taken as constant.** A silicon diode's forward characteristic
is very steep: once conducting, its voltage barely changes with current ✓ Treating it as
a fixed 0·2 V (0·3 V for germanium, 0·7 V for silicon in most textbooks) is the standard
first approximation.
**Why the diode must be forward biased.** The current flows in the direction the diode's
arrow points ✓ Were it reverse biased, no current would flow at all and the question
would have no answer.
**A check on the arithmetic.** 0·2 mA through 10 kΩ total resistance:
V = 0·2 x 10 = **2 V** ✓ with the milli and the kilo cancelling - a useful shortcut,
since mA x kΩ = V.
**Reading the distractors.** **2·0 V** would be the answer if the diode were an ideal
conductor, dropping nothing - but it is not among the options; **1·3 V** ✗ and **0·5 V**
✗ account for only part of the path. **0** ✗ would need no current at all ✓
∴ 2.2 V.

A carburettor draws fuel into the airstream by the **pressure drop at a constriction** -
Bernoulli's principle.
**Step 1 — state the principle.** Along a streamline,
P + ½ρv² + ρgh = **constant** ✓
so where the speed is **high**, the pressure is **low**.
**Step 2 — apply it to the carburettor.** Air rushing to the engine passes through a
narrow throat - the **venturi** ✓ By continuity (Av = constant) the air **speeds up**
there, and by Bernoulli the pressure **falls** below atmospheric.
**Step 3 — see what that does.** The fuel jet opens into the throat, and the reduced
pressure **sucks petrol** out of the float chamber, which is at atmospheric pressure ✓
The faster the engine breathes, the lower the throat pressure and the more fuel is
drawn - so the mixture ratio stays roughly right across the speed range.
**Why this is self-regulating.** Both the air flow and the fuel flow increase together ✓
The device delivers the correct **proportion** of fuel to air automatically, which is
exactly what the question describes.
**Other applications of the same effect.**
the **venturi meter**, which measures flow rate from the pressure drop ✓
the **atomiser** or spray gun, and the perfume bulb
the **Bunsen burner**, drawing air into the gas stream
the **aerofoil**, where faster flow over the curved upper surface gives lift ✓
the curve of a spinning cricket ball
**A worked estimate.** Air at 50 m s⁻¹ in the throat, with ρ = 1·2 kg m⁻³:
ΔP = ½(1·2)(2500) = **1500 Pa** below atmospheric ✓ enough to lift petrol about 20 cm -
ample for the jet.
**Why the other principles do not apply.**
**Pascal's law** ✗ concerns pressure transmission in a **static** fluid, as in a
hydraulic lift.
**Newton's law of cooling** ✗ is about heat loss, not fluids.
**Archimedes' principle** ✗ is about buoyancy ✓ None of them involves the
speed-pressure relationship that makes a carburettor work.
∴ Bernoulli's Principle.

A **transverse** wave needs the medium to resist **shear**, and a gas cannot.
**Step 1 — recall what each wave requires.**
a **longitudinal** wave propagates by alternate **compression and rarefaction**, so it
needs only a **bulk modulus** ✓
a **transverse** wave propagates by **sideways displacement** of layers, so it needs a
**modulus of rigidity** - the ability to resist shear ✓
**Step 2 — look at air.** A gas has a bulk modulus - it resists being compressed - but
its modulus of rigidity is **zero** ✓ Layers of air slide over one another with no
restoring force whatever, so there is nothing to carry a transverse disturbance back.
**Step 3 — conclude.** Sound in air must be **longitudinal**, because **air has no
modulus of rigidity** ✓
**What happens in a solid.** Solids have **both** moduli, so they carry **both** kinds of
wave ✓ and the longitudinal one travels faster, since
v_long = √[(K + 4G/3)/ρ] and v_trans = √(G/ρ)
**How seismology uses this.** An earthquake sends out **P waves** (longitudinal, fast)
and **S waves** (transverse, slower) ✓ S waves **cannot** pass through the Earth's
liquid outer core - and the resulting S-wave shadow zone is the principal evidence that
the core is molten. The same physics, on a planetary scale.
**The speed of sound in air.**
v = √(γP/ρ) ✓
Laplace's formula, with γ the ratio of specific heats, giving about **340 m s⁻¹** at
room temperature. Newton's earlier isothermal version, √(P/ρ), gave 280 m s⁻¹ and was
about 16% low - the discrepancy resolved when Laplace realised the compressions are
**adiabatic**, not isothermal.
**Why the other explanations fail.**
"**air is a mixture of gases**" ✗ - a pure gas behaves identically.
"**density of air is very small**" ✗ - density affects the **speed**, not the type of
wave.
"**inherent characteristics of sound waves**" ✗ - this merely restates the fact without
explaining it; sound **is** transverse in some contexts (surface waves), so the property
belongs to the **medium** ✓
∴ air does not have a modulus of rigidity.

Hydrostatic pressure depends only on the **depth**, not on the shape or the amount of
liquid.
**Step 1 — state the formula.**
P = P₀ + **hρg** ✓
The only variable is h, the vertical depth below the free surface.
**Step 2 — read the figure.** The two vessels have **different shapes** - one flares
out, the other is narrower - but the water stands at the **same level** in both ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** Same depth, same density, same g, so the pressure at the bottom
is **the same** in both ✓
**Why the shape makes no difference.** Pressure at a point in a fluid is the same in
**all directions**, and it is transmitted sideways as well as downwards ✓ The sloping
walls of the wider vessel support the extra weight of the liquid above them; that weight
is carried by the **walls**, not by the base.
**The hydrostatic paradox.** The force on the base of the wider vessel is **larger**,
because the base has a larger area:
F = PA ✓
but the **pressure** - force per unit area - is identical. The weight of liquid in each
vessel may differ greatly; the pressure does not.
**Pascal's vases.** The classic demonstration uses several vessels of wildly different
shapes mounted on a common base ✓ Fill them and the liquid stands at the **same level**
in every one, and the pressure gauge reads the same for each.
**A worked instance.** Both vessels filled to 0·5 m:
P = 1000 x 9·8 x 0·5 = **4900 Pa** above atmospheric ✓ in each, whatever their width.
**Why the answer would change if the levels differed.** Then h would differ and so would
the pressure ✓ It is the equality of the **levels**, not of the volumes, that settles
this question.
**Reading the distractors.** Options claiming one pressure is **greater** ✗ confuse
pressure with total weight or with volume. The option saying pressure **depends on the
shape** ✗ states the misconception the question is designed to expose ✓
∴ the pressure on the bottom of (a) and (b) is the same.

Hydraulic stress acts **all over** a body, so the modulus relating it to the resulting
strain is the **bulk modulus**.
**Step 1 — recall the three moduli.**
**Young's modulus** Y = tensile stress/longitudinal strain - stretching a wire ✓
**bulk modulus** K = hydraulic (volume) stress/volume strain - squeezing on all sides ✓
**rigidity modulus** G = shearing stress/shearing strain - sliding one face over another
**Step 2 — identify hydraulic stress.** It is a uniform pressure applied over the whole
surface, as when a body is immersed in a fluid ✓ The body's **volume** changes while
its shape does not.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The ratio is the **bulk modulus** ✓
**The formula.**
K = −P/(ΔV/V) ✓
with the minus sign because an increase in pressure **reduces** the volume, so that K
comes out positive.
**Why compressibility is the wrong answer.** It is the **reciprocal**:
compressibility = **1/K** ✓ It measures how easily a substance is squeezed, not the
ratio asked for. This is the designed trap.
**Typical values.**
water: K ≈ **2·2 x 10⁹ Pa** - nearly incompressible, which is why hydraulic systems
work ✓
steel: K ≈ **1·6 x 10¹¹ Pa**
air at atmospheric pressure: K ≈ **10⁵ Pa**, a million times smaller than water's -
which is why gases are compressible and liquids are not.
**Why gases need two bulk moduli.**
isothermal: **K = P**
adiabatic: **K = γP** ✓
and it is the adiabatic value that governs the speed of sound, as Laplace showed.
**The one modulus that applies to all three states.** Only the **bulk** modulus ✓
Solids have all three; **liquids and gases have only K**, since they cannot sustain a
shear stress at all - which is also why they carry no transverse waves.
**Reading the distractors.** **Young's modulus** ✗ concerns stretching in one direction.
**Rigidity modulus** ✗ concerns shear. **Compressibility** ✗ is 1/K ✓
∴ Bulk modulus.

Young's modulus is the ratio of **tensile stress** to **longitudinal strain**.
**Step 1 — define the two quantities.**
**tensile stress** = F/A, the stretching force per unit cross-sectional area, in Pa ✓
**longitudinal strain** = ΔL/L, the fractional change in length - a pure number ✓
**Step 2 — form the ratio.**
**Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(A ΔL)** ✓
with units of **pascals**, the same as stress, since strain is dimensionless.
**Step 3 — note where it applies.** Only within the **elastic limit**, where Hooke's law
holds and the body returns to its original length when the load is removed ✓ Beyond that
the stress-strain curve bends over and Y loses its meaning.
**What Y measures.** The **stiffness** of a material in tension ✓ A high Y means a
material that stretches very little under load.
**Typical values.**
steel: **2 x 10¹¹ Pa** ✓
copper: 1·1 x 10¹¹
glass: 0·6 x 10¹¹
rubber: about **10⁶ Pa** - a hundred thousand times smaller, which is why it stretches
so visibly
**Why steel is used for cables and rubber is not.** A high Y means a small extension
for a given load ✓ A steel cable 1 m long and 1 mm² in section stretches only 0·05 mm
under 100 N.
**The complete family of moduli.**
**Y**: tensile stress/longitudinal strain ✓
**K**: hydraulic stress/volume strain
**G**: shearing stress/shearing strain ✓
and they are linked, for an isotropic solid, through **Poisson's ratio**.
**Why only solids have a Young's modulus.** Fluids cannot be put in **tension** in this
way ✓ They have a bulk modulus only.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Hydraulic stress and hydraulic strain**" ✗ defines the
**bulk** modulus. "**Shearing stress and shearing strain**" ✗ defines the **rigidity**
modulus. "**Bulk stress and longitudinal strain**" ✗ mismatches a stress of one kind
with a strain of another, and defines nothing ✓
∴ tensile stress and longitudinal strain.
